cards.front: Distinguish **state**, **regime**, and **government** — and rank them by how enduring each is.
cards.back:
**State** — the ongoing **administrative apparatus** (ch. 2); the *most* enduring.
**Regime** — the formal **+ informal** institutions defining the **type** of government; more enduring than governments, less than the state.
**Government** — the **current occupants** of office; least enduring.

*Illustration:* the US = **46 administrations but one democratic regime** since 1789; **Nigeria = 8 regimes**.

cards.front: Define **citizen** vs **subject** — and say what historical shift created the citizen.
cards.back:
**Citizen** = a member of the political community with **rights + duties**.
**Subject** = a person with **duties (obedience) only** — no mechanism to protect "rights."

200–300 years ago Europeans were **subjects** of absolutist monarchs; the citizen arose as **sovereignty moved from the monarch to "the people"** (after the French Revolution people addressed each other as *"citizen"*).

cards.front: State **Marshall's (1963) three rights of citizenship** — and the condition for "full" citizenship.
cards.back:
**① Civil** — individual freedom, fair treatment.
**② Political** — participation, the vote.
**③ Social** — welfare, socioeconomic equality.

Full citizenship needs *enough* **social** equality to make civil/political equality real. **Virtually no country fully provides all three.**

cards.front: Name the concept: **organised, nongovernmental, nonviolent activity by groups larger than families or firms** — impossible under absolutism.
cards.back:
**Civil society.**

It was **enabled by religious pluralism + capitalism** and is *impossible under absolutism*. Related: **popular sovereignty** — even dictators claim to rule *on behalf of* the people (theocracy claims God willed the exception).
cards.hint: Bigger than the family, smaller than the state.

cards.front: Walk up the **V-Dem "Regimes of the World" ladder** (Lührmann, Tannenberg & Lindberg 2018): what test separates each of the four rungs?
cards.back:
**Closed autocracy** — *no* multi-party elections.
↓ (add elections)
**Electoral autocracy** — multi-party elections, but **not free & fair** (restrictions undermine fairness).
↓ (make elections free & fair)
**Electoral democracy** — free & fair elections; **partial** rights/checks.
↓ (add rights, legal equality & checks on the executive)
**Liberal democracy** — free & fair elections **+ rights, legal equality, checks**.

cards.front: On the V-Dem ladder: **multi-party elections are held, but restrictions make them *not* free & fair, and there are no real checks on the executive.** Which rung is this?
cards.back:
**Electoral autocracy.**

It sits *above* **closed autocracy** (which has no multi-party elections) and *below* **electoral democracy** (whose elections *are* free & fair). The classic OD case that fits is **Mexico under the PRI**.

cards.front: The chapter's **red thread**: what single question orders *every* regime type, and how does liberal democracy answer it?
cards.back:
**"How is power shared between citizens and the state?"**

**Liberal democracy** shares it *widely* (limited government + Marshall's three rights) and is the **benchmark**. Every other regime **tilts power toward the state** and restricts full citizenship to a select group (the working class / loyal nationals / the developers / the faithful). For each type ask: **who has power, and what rights do citizens get?**
cards.hint: One axis: citizens vs the state.

cards.front: Define **liberal democracy**, and give **Dahl's 8 guarantees** (the working definition).
cards.back:
**Liberal democracy = democracy (rule by the people) + liberalism (individual rights)** — a *limited* state that protects rights and holds free, competitive elections.

**Dahl's 8 guarantees:** freedom of **association** · **expression** · right to **vote** · broad **office eligibility** · leaders' right to **compete** · alternative **information** · **free & fair elections** · institutions that make policy **depend on votes**.

cards.front: Distinguish the **three varieties of democracy** — liberal, social, participatory — with a country for each.
cards.back:
**Liberal** — political rights (**UK**).
**Social democracy** — adds **economic regulation + social rights** (**Sweden**); a variant *within* liberal democracy.
**Participatory** — **direct involvement beyond voting** (**Switzerland**).

*Roots:* liberalism arose in the 16th–17th-c. religious wars; **Locke** — govt is legitimate only if it preserves **life, liberty, property**. Democracy was added *later* (early liberals limited citizenship to **male property owners**).

cards.front: **Free individuals contract to be governed, and government is legitimate only so long as it preserves their natural rights.** Name this theory, its key thinkers, and Locke's three rights.
cards.back:
**Social contract theory** — **Hobbes, Locke, Montesquieu, Rousseau**.

**Locke:** government is legitimate only if it preserves **life, liberty, property** (Jefferson → *"life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness"*). It's the intellectual root of **liberalism** / liberal democracy.

cards.front: List the **seven ideology-based regime types** and, in a word or two, **who has power** in each.
cards.back:
**① Liberal democracy** — the **legislature** (elected, removable).
**② Communism** — the **vanguard party**.
**③ Fascism** — a **supreme leader**.
**④ Modernizing authoritarianism** — a **modern (educated) elite**.
**⑤ Personalist** — an **individual ruler**.
**⑥ Electoral authoritarianism** — the **ruling party** (via rigged elections).
**⑦ Theocracy** — **God** (via the clergy) — not the people.

Each is defined by an **ideology** answering *who has power* and *what citizens get*.
cards.hint: Legislature · party · leader · elite · ruler · ruling party · God.

cards.front: **Economic forces drive history; capitalism yields to a proletarian revolution and, eventually, a classless, stateless society — ruled meanwhile by a vanguard party.** Which regime/ideology, and what did it produce in practice?
cards.back:
**Communism** (**Marx's historical materialism**): *feudalism → capitalism → socialism → communism*. Liberal rights = *"equal rights for unequal people."*

**Stages:** **socialism** = collective ownership + **dictatorship of the proletariat** (a *class* dictatorship) → stateless, classless **communism**.

*In practice* it produced the **totalitarian state** (any theory promising utopia tends that way) — see **Russia/Stalin**.
cards.hint: Historical materialism; vanguard party now, utopia "later."

cards.front: **Antiliberal *and* anticommunist: society is organic, the *state creates the nation*, and the individual exists only for the state — so citizens have duties, not rights.** Which regime, and its two hallmark features?
cards.back:
**Fascism.** A **supreme leader** embodies the nation.

**Hallmarks:** ① **organic** conception of society (individual exists for the state) · ② **corporatism** — one state-controlled organisation per sector (one union, one business association). It rejects rationality/materialism, glorifies struggle & war → **totalitarian** (Nazi Germany).
cards.hint: The state makes the nation; corporatism.

cards.front: **Legitimacy comes from *development, not rights*: a modern educated elite must guide progress, and democracy would only interfere.** Name the regime type and its **four institutional forms**.
cards.back:
**Modernizing authoritarianism** — **technocratic legitimacy** rooted in **modernization theory**.

**Four forms:** ① **one-party** (civilian; postcolonial Africa/Asia — **Tanzania**) · ② **military** (coup — **Brazil**) · ③ **bureaucratic-authoritarian** · ④ **personalist**.

cards.front: **In the weakest states, one leader captures everything — even the party or military that raised him — through personal patron–client loyalty rather than institutions.** Which regime type, and what is the mechanism called?
cards.back:
**Personalist regime** — the mechanism is **neopatrimonialism** (rule via **personal patron–client loyalty**, not institutions).

Weak, unstable, unpredictable; rule of law is inconsistent. Most common in Africa (Mobutu, Marcos, **Abacha/Nigeria**).

cards.front: **Real opposition and elections exist — but the ruling party manipulates the rules so it never actually loses, while proclaiming itself democratic.** Which regime type, and why did it spread after the Cold War?
cards.back:
**Electoral authoritarianism** (a **hybrid**) — blends liberal-democratic (elections) + modernizing-authoritarian ("stability/development") legitimacy.

It **spread after the Cold War** because *open* authoritarianism lost international legitimacy — so autocrats adopted a **democratic veneer** (see **Mexico/PRI**).
cards.hint: A democratic shell over a rigged game.

cards.front: **Rule by religious authorities on behalf of God, so ultimate sovereignty is Allah's, not the people's.** Name the regime, its modern ideology, and the key Islamist terms.
cards.back:
**Theocracy** — modern ideology is **Islamism** (a 19th–20th-c. *reaction to Western imperialism*, **not** traditional): **sharia** as the basis of government.

**Key terms:** **sharia** (law) · **ijtihad** (individual interpretation) vs **taqlid** (blind acceptance) · **shura** (consultation — the opening for quasi-democracy) · **umma** (community) · **jihad** (three kinds: inner struggle [most important] → righting injustice → armed defence [least]). **Iran** is the world's *only true theocracy*.
cards.hint: God is sovereign; sharia, shura, umma, jihad.

cards.front: Match each **"who has power"** to its regime type: (a) an educated modern elite guiding development; (b) a vanguard party; (c) a supreme leader embodying the nation; (d) clergy acting for God.
cards.back:
(a) **Modernizing authoritarianism.**
(b) **Communism.**
(c) **Fascism.**
(d) **Theocracy.**

Each differs only in *who is trusted with power* and *what ideology justifies it* — the taxonomy's organising move.

cards.front: **A liberal democracy that evolved *gradually* — no single written constitution, no revolutionary break from monarchy — via Magna Carta (1215) → Glorious Revolution (1688) → Bill of Rights (1689).** Which case, and what informal institution anchors its power?
cards.back:
**United Kingdom** — the *"cradle of democracy,"* the **first liberal democracy**.

Power rests on **parliamentary sovereignty** (a powerful *informal* institution) + the slow build-up of all three **Marshall rights** (franchise expanded only under pressure — 1832; women 1918; devolution 1997; a standalone Supreme Court 2005).

cards.front: **A revolution in the "wrong country" (agrarian, not advanced-capitalist); Lenin adds the vanguard party (Oct 1917), Stalin builds a totalitarian state (2–20m deaths), Gorbachev's reforms end it (Dec 1991).** Which case, and what does it prove about ideology vs practice?
cards.back:
**Russia/USSR** — the first *"communist"* regime.

It shows communism in practice = the **totalitarian state**, and that a regime can **diverge wildly from its ideology**: the chain **Marx → Lenin → Stalin** drifted far from Marx's theory. (Now Russia is **electoral authoritarian**.)

cards.front: **A leader *elected, not by coup* — his party won 37% (1932) amid depression — then used the Reichstag fire (1933) → Enabling Act to build a dictatorship, replacing unions with a party front.** Which case and regime type?
cards.back:
**Germany — the rise of the Nazis** = **fascism** + the **totalitarian state**.

Nazism fused fascism with **racism** → the **Holocaust (~6m Jews)**. Its horror **delegitimised fascism globally**, though **neofascism** persists (Le Pen's National Front — 2nd in France's 2002 presidential race).
cards.hint: Elected, not a coup; Reichstag fire.

cards.front: Two **modernizing-authoritarian** cases: (a) a US-backed 1964 coup installing a technocratic military that staked legitimacy on the "Brazilian Miracle"; (b) a civilian "philosopher-king" who justified a one-party state and *ujamaa* socialism. Name both.
cards.back:
(a) **Brazil (1964–85)** — **military** modernizing authoritarianism (National Security Doctrine, development + anticommunism). When growth stalled → **democracy restored 1985**. *No growth = no legitimacy.*
(b) **Tanzania — Julius Nyerere** — **one-party** (civilian) form; *ujamaa* ruined agriculture but achieved **near-universal literacy**; he **voluntarily resigned (1985)**. The *development vs democracy* trade-off.

cards.front: **After the military annulled the 1993 election, a general seized power, gutted the courts, hanged the poet Ken Saro-Wiwa, and looted ~$3 billion via oil patronage — until his sudden 1998 death ended it.** Which case and regime type?
cards.back:
**Nigeria — General Abacha (1993–98)** = a **personalist** regime.

He ruled by **neopatrimonial** oil patronage; a weak state's institutions crumbled around one man. Wary officers then delivered the **democracy in place since 1999**.

cards.front: **A party ruled ~71 years via regular *but rigged* elections — a democratic veneer over clientelism, corporatism and fraud — until an opposition candidate finally broke the monopoly in 2000.** Which case and regime type?
cards.back:
**Mexico — the PRI** = the classic **electoral authoritarianism**.

Informal institutions (**clientelism, fraud**) dominated the formal democratic shell; power rotated among factions, presidents limited to one **sexenio** (Tlatelolco Massacre 1968). **Vicente Fox (PAN) broke the monopoly in 2000.**

cards.front: **A 1979 revolution built the first modern theocracy: a cleric Supreme Leader + a 12-clergy Guardian Council vet all candidates and laws, sitting *above* an elected president and parliament.** Which case, and what tension defines it?
cards.back:
**Iran — the Islamic Republic** (Khomeini's **1979 revolution**).

The **1979 constitution** makes **Allah sovereign** and sharia the sole law. It runs on a permanent tension between **theocratic authority** (Supreme Leader, Guardian Council) and **quasi-democratic** elements (*shura* / elections to the **Majlis**).
cards.hint: Supreme Leader + Guardian Council above elected bodies.

cards.front: Explain **regime *change*** through the **Interests / Beliefs / Structures** lens (the same lens from Lecture 1) — one line each.
cards.back:
**Interests** — elites expand/restrict democracy to **maximise power** (democratise post-1990 for aid; **backslide** when power is threatened).
**Beliefs** — democratic ideals spread in the 19th–20th c.; **fascism/communism** caused reversals; recent **populism** erodes liberal values.
**Structures** — **industrialisation** enabled democratisation; **Cold War blocs** sustained autocracy; **globalisation/inequality** now strain democracy.

cards.front: Define three cross-cutting terms: **totalitarian state**, **corporatism**, **technocratic legitimacy**.
cards.back:
**Totalitarian state** — controls **~all of society** and **eliminates civil society** (the endpoint of both communism and fascism in practice).
**Corporatism** — **one state-controlled organisation per social sector** (one union, one business association) — a fascist hallmark.
**Technocratic legitimacy** — the right to rule based on **expertise** — the basis of modernizing authoritarianism.
cards.hint: Total control · one org per sector · rule by expertise.

cards.front: State the chapter's **recurring thread about ideology** — and why *informal* institutions matter for classifying real regimes.
cards.back:
**No regime works exactly as its ideology claims** — regimes routinely **diverge** from their ideology, and **informal institutions** (patronage, factions, parliamentary sovereignty, clientelism) often explain how a regime *really* works, especially in **weak states**.

That's why *~90% of the world's constitutions — including authoritarian ones — mention "democracy"* (Elkins et al. 2014): liberal democracy is the **benchmark everyone responds to**, even when they don't practise it.
cards.hint: Ideology on paper ≠ informal institutions in practice.
